props.title: The Way I See It

sections.content: **The Way I See It (2020)** (2020) offers an unprecedented look at the Obama presidency through the lens of Pete Souza's photography, joining other intimate political documentaries like **The Final Year** (2017) and **Weiner** (2016). Director Dawn Porter crafts a dual narrative that both chronicles Souza's evolution from photojournalist to social media activist and provides a stark visual contrast between presidential administrations. The film's power comes from Souza's unprecedented access - he shot nearly 2 million photos during Obama's eight years - allowing viewers to witness historic moments and private gestures that humanize the presidency.

sections.content: The film exists in conversation with other documentaries that examine the intersection of politics and image-making. **JFK: The Lost Bullet** (2011) analyzes the Zapruder film, while **The Reagan Show** (2017) explores how Ronald Reagan's team masterfully crafted his public image. Souza's work reveals how official photography shapes historical narrative, much like the way **Our Nixon** (2013) used Super 8 home movies to show a different side of the Nixon White House.

Porter's direction particularly shines in juxtaposing Souza's Obama-era photos with current events, creating powerful visual essays about leadership and empathy. This approach recalls similar techniques in **The Kingmaker** (2019) and **Get Me Roger Stone** (2017), where archival footage is weaponized to expose political contrasts. The film's examination of how photography shapes public perception connects to media-focused documentaries like **Page One: Inside the New York Times** (2011). sections.content: The film's exploration of White House photography builds on a rich documentary tradition examining political image-making. **Jackie: A Tale of Two Sisters** (2017) showed how Jackie Kennedy carefully controlled the Kennedy visual narrative, while **The Perfect Candidate** (2019) demonstrated how social media has transformed political imagery. Souza's transition from observer to activist mirrors the journey seen in **Hail Satan?** (2019), where documentation leads to advocacy.
